data.headline: A faint source that shifts position between every epoch

motion.method: Simulated centroid difference between Epoch 1 and Epoch 2 in the aligned frame

explanations.label: A known asteroid or comet
explanations.description: Most moving points in survey images are already-catalogued small bodies.
explanations.rationale: No counterpart was found in the simulated catalogue of known objects. Real catalogues are incomplete for faint bodies, and a main-belt asteroid near a turning point of its apparent path can also move this slowly for a few days.

explanations.label: A distant icy body beyond Neptune
explanations.description: Trans-Neptunian objects drift slowly because they are far away.
explanations.rationale: The measured drift of about 0.23 arcseconds per hour is slow, as expected for a distant body. Being consistent is not the same as being identified: no orbit can be fitted from three positions.

explanations.label: An undiscovered planet
explanations.description: For example the hypothesised, unconfirmed "Planet Nine".
explanations.rationale: Nothing in this evidence singles out a planet over any other slow-moving body. Establishing a new solar-system object needs many positions over months to years, an orbit, and independent confirmation.

explanations.label: An image artifact or noise
explanations.description: Cosmic-ray hits, hot pixels and ghosts can look like sources.
explanations.rationale: The source is detected in two wavelength bands at all three epochs with similar brightness. Artifacts rarely repeat that way.

explanations.label: A variable star or galaxy
explanations.description: A fixed source whose brightness changes.
explanations.rationale: A variable source stays in the same place. This one changes position, leaving a paired dark-and-bright signature in the difference image.

explanations.label: Image misalignment
explanations.description: If two images are not registered correctly, every star appears to shift.
explanations.rationale: Neighbouring stars subtract cleanly. The alignment residual is about 0.06 pixels, while this source moved 8.6 pixels.

evidence.title: Paired residual in the difference image
evidence.summary: Epoch 2 minus Epoch 1 shows a negative (blue) residual at the earlier position and a positive (amber) residual 53 arcseconds away.

evidence.title: Apparent motion between Epoch 1 and Epoch 2
evidence.summary: Positions measured by the (simulated) backend in the aligned frame.

evidence.title: Detected in two bands at every epoch
evidence.summary: Six independent detections (Band 2 and Band 4, three epochs) at signal-to-noise above 10.

evidence.title: No match in the known-object catalogue
evidence.summary: A simulated cross-match against known solar-system objects returned nothing within 30 arcseconds at any epoch. The real backend will query actual catalogues.

evidence.title: Spectrum resembling sunlight reflected from an icy surface
evidence.summary: The simulated spectrum follows a Sun-like continuum with injected absorption near 1.5, 2.0 and 3.0 µm.

followUp: More positions over weeks to months, to fit an orbit and estimate distance.
A cross-match against catalogues of known solar-system objects at each observation time.
A search along the predicted track in other SPHEREx exposures (IRSA provides a Moving Object Search Tool for known orbits).
Independent confirmation with a different telescope.
limitations: This candidate is simulated. It exists to demonstrate the workflow and is not evidence of any real object.
Three positions cannot constrain an orbit.
Each exposure samples a different wavelength, so brightness differences between epochs mix colour and time variation.

provenance.origin: Injected into the simulated images by the SkyShift X simulator.
provenance.notes: Synthetic test data that mimics the structure of SPHEREx products. Not a NASA measurement.
